headline: Ashwagandha
for lifters.
dek: A new trial, a cautious meta-analysis and a men-only study: what the research on ashwagandha and strength shows.
photoAlt: A coach with a whistle holds a clipboard.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Nov 3, 2026 · Clinical review pending

pull.quote: Current evidence does not establish that adjunctive ashwagandha meaningfully enhances resistance-training adaptations

body: [[/ashwagandha|Ashwagandha]] is a shrub, Withania somnifera, in the nightshade family, and its root has long been used in India’s Ayurvedic medicine.[^dtu][^dk] Three pieces of research from the past few months show what has actually been measured in people who lift: a new randomized trial, a meta-analysis of the trials that paired the root with resistance training, and a men-only trial that has just begun to be listed.

The trial, published on September 9, 2026, in Frontiers in Nutrition, was randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled. Of 84 people enrolled, 83 finished: 41 on the extract and 42 on placebo. They were aged 25 to 50 and took either a 300 mg capsule of a sustained-release ashwagandha root extract or a placebo capsule once a day for 90 days.[^trial] The group included both men and non-pregnant women, all with a body mass index between 25.0 and 29.9, who were recreationally active and in the first month of strength training.[^trialft] Everyone followed the same exercise plan, five training days a week alternating resistance and aerobic sessions.[^trialft]

The researchers measured the one-repetition maximum on the bench press, maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max), testosterone, two muscle-damage markers and quality of life.[^trial] Both groups improved; the extract group improved more. By day 91, its bench-press maximum had risen by 15.31 kg against 7.33 kg on placebo, and VO2max by 30.56 against 18.14 mL/kg/min, both with p below 0.001; the gap was already present at day 30.[^trial] The authors described the extra VO2max gain as a “very large effect”[^trialft] and concluded that three months of the extract improved strength, endurance and overall well-being in recreationally active adults.[^trial]

Testosterone is where the headline figures need care. Among the men taking the extract, mean total testosterone rose from 315.63 to 437.07 ng/dL, an increase of 121.43 ng/dL, and that rise within the group was statistically significant (p = 0.024). Among the men on placebo it rose from 332.00 to 400.43 ng/dL, which was not significant on its own.[^trialft] But when the two groups were compared directly, the paper reports that “between group differences were not statistically significant for both total and free testosterone concentrations”.[^trialft] Put plainly: testosterone rose within the treated group, but it did not rise more than on placebo.

On safety, 16 people reported mild, short-lived side effects: six on the extract (three with gastritis, three with muscle pain) and ten on placebo. All resolved, and the investigators judged them unlikely to be caused by the study product.[^trialft] The authors named their own limits as a narrow body-weight range, “relatively modest sample size and single-center study design.”[^trialft] The funding is stated in the paper: the work was funded by Nutriventia Private Limited, which also made the capsules, and three authors are its employees; the funder took part in the study design, the writing and the decision to publish.[^trialft]

The meta-analysis, published on August 27, 2026, in Nutrients by researchers at Dongshin University in South Korea, looked only at randomized trials that combined a standardized extract with structured resistance training in healthy adults. It found four; three, with 161 people, could be pooled. Ashwagandha was associated with larger gains than placebo in bench-press and lower-body maximums, but when a stricter statistical method was applied both strength results lost significance, and each leaned on one influential trial. The authors rated the certainty of both strength findings as low.[^meta] Their conclusion: “Current evidence does not establish that adjunctive ashwagandha meaningfully enhances resistance-training adaptations”.[^meta] They called for “Adequately powered, independently funded RCTs using direct measures of hypertrophy”.[^meta] The review had no outside funding.[^meta]

Wider reviews point the same way. A June 2026 meta-analysis of 13 trials with 599 participants found the most consistent evidence for aerobic endurance, while strength effects were “positive but uncertain”.[^li] A February 2026 review of 23 hormone trials, with 1,706 participants, reported that ashwagandha raised testosterone in men by a mean of 57.43 ng/dL compared with placebo.[^fornalik]

The newest study answers part of that call. A trial run by the Gdansk University of Physical Education and Sport in Poland, first posted on ClinicalTrials.gov on September 3, 2026, plans to enroll 40 healthy, non-smoking men aged 25 to 40 who already train with weights. They are to take 400 mg a day of a standardized root extract (5% withanolides) or a starch placebo for 12 weeks, while lifting three times a week. Its main measures are bench-press strength, cortisol and BDNF, a protein linked to brain function; testosterone is measured as well. It is recruiting, with main results expected in 2027.[^ctg]

What is still unknown is long-term safety and whether the gains last. The largest safety trial so far gave 600 mg a day or placebo to 1,002 adults with stress and anxiety for eight weeks, and found no serious adverse events and no significant liver-test changes compared with placebo.[^safety] Case reports describe something rarer. In five patients from Iceland and the US, jaundice began two to 12 weeks after starting ashwagandha supplements; liver tests returned to normal within one to five months in four, and one was lost to follow-up.[^bjornsson] In an Indian series of eight people who took single-ingredient products, three with existing chronic liver disease developed liver failure and died.[^philips]

Regulators differ. In the US, ashwagandha is sold as a dietary supplement, and FDA says it “does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed.”[^suppqa] Denmark’s food agency says products containing it are illegal to sell there, citing a risk assessment that found harmful effects on sex hormones and reproduction.[^dk] In the UK, the Committee on Toxicity discussed a third draft statement on ashwagandha in September 2026.[^cot] It is not on the World Anti-Doping Agency’s prohibited list.[^wada]

The published record so far is a handful of small, short trials, the newest funded by the extract’s maker, showing larger strength and fitness gains than placebo, pooled evidence rated low certainty, a [[/testosterone|testosterone]] rise that did not separate from placebo in the newest trial, and an independent men-only trial still under way.
